## The idea

Two melodies become *polyphony* when your ear can follow them as independent
voices. Independence requires more than different pitches. Each voice needs its
own rhythm, contour, register, and place in the phrase. If both parts attack
together with the same durations, one tends to sound like chord filling.

Sonic Pi maps this musical idea onto concurrency. A live_loop or in_thread gives
each voice its own process. cue sends a timing event, and sync waits for it.
Deterministic scheduling keeps the processes on the same beat grid, provided
each one sleeps for the duration it claims.

Keep the score for each voice in a separate structure. Shared tempo and bar
length are useful. Shared mutable note arrays are a source of obscure bugs,
especially when one loop rotates or changes an array while another reads it.

## Run this

A clock loop announces each four-beat bar. The melody and bass wait for the same
announcement, then consume independent score data whose durations each total
four beats.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88

melody = [
  {note: :e4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :g4, start: 1.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: :a4, start: 1.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: :b4, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
]

bass = [
  {note: :e2, start: 0.0, duration: 2.0},
  {note: :d2, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :b1, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0}
]

define :play_events do |events, synth_name, amp|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.8, amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

live_loop :bar_clock do
  cue :bar
  sleep 4
end

live_loop :upper_voice do
  sync :bar
  play_events melody, :piano, 0.9
end

live_loop :lower_voice do
  sync :bar
  play_events bass, :fm, 0.55
end
```

After the loops meet at a bar cue, they repeat without cumulative drift. The
bass changes on a different attack pattern from the melody, so it remains
audible as a line.

## Change one thing

1. Change the last bass duration from 1.0 to 0.75. The lower loop reaches sync
   early and waits for the next bar cue. Listen for the quarter-beat silence.
   The voices do not drift, but the broken invariant becomes audible.
2. Give the bass the melody's duration pattern while retaining its pitches.
   The parts align at every attack. Listen for the texture becoming more like a
   harmonised melody and less like two lines.
3. Transpose the melody up twelve semitones by changing each note to
   note(event[:note]) + 12 inside a separate renderer. The wider register makes
   the voices easier to track without changing their rhythmic relationship.

## Why it works

Each voice is a state machine with one responsibility: play its next event,
advance to the next absolute start, and meet the shared bar boundary. The
`:note`, `:start`, and `:duration` keys retain the general event schema from the
transcription lessons. The clock loop is coordination, not score storage. This
distinction keeps a change to the melody from altering the bass process.

Sonic Pi schedules musical time independently of how long Ruby takes to execute
ordinary lines. A sixteen-bar test should therefore return to the same cue
without gradual separation. A wrong sleep total produces a repeatable gap or
late arrival instead of floating-point drift. That makes duration sums the
first diagnostic.

sync also defines a musical boundary. Bar cues suit repeating grooves. Phrase
cues suit sections whose lengths differ. Too many cues couple the voices at
every note and erase the benefit of independent processes. Coordinate at the
largest boundary that still keeps the form stable.

The example runs indefinitely, so stop it with Cmd-. or Alt-. The Ruby syntax
can be checked outside Sonic Pi, while timing, balance, and the audible
independence of the voices remain manual listening work.

## Take it further

Build an eight-bar two-part arrangement and let it repeat for sixteen bars.
Store upper and lower events in separate arrays, validate each bar total, and
use one cue per bar or phrase. Give the voices different attack patterns and a
register gap of at least an octave. The target is a loop that stays locked while
either line can be muted, transposed, or replaced without editing the other
voice's score.
